ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a 3×3 grid composed of nine equal small squares. Both slanted lines start from the lower-left corner of the whole grid; the lower slanted line reaches a position on the right boundary of the grid two squares high from the bottom side; the higher slanted line reaches a position on the top boundary of the grid two squares away from the left side. α is marked between the bottom horizontal line and the lower slanted line, and β is marked between the two slanted lines. Reasoning: Let the lower-left corner be the coordinate origin (0,0), and let the side length of each small square be 1. The lower slanted line passes through the point (3,2), so tan α = 2/3. Let the angle between the higher slanted line and the bottom horizontal line be θ; it passes through the point (2,3), so tan θ = 3/2. Because tan α · tan θ = (2/3)(3/2)=1, and α and θ are both acute angles, α+θ=90°. Also, because θ is the angle from the bottom side to the higher slanted line, and it is composed of α and β, θ=α+β. Substituting gives α+(α+β)=90°, namely 2α+β=90°.

raw_record.question_text: In the diagram made up of nine squares, what equation between $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is definitely true for the marked angle?

method.method_draft: Use a coordinate/slope approach. From the image, model the 3-by-3 square grid with the common vertex of the two slanted segments at the bottom-left corner, coordinates (0,0). Read the lower ray as ending at the right side of the grid at the horizontal gridline two squares up, i.e. at (3,2), so its angle from the bottom side is α and tan α = 2/3. Read the upper ray as ending on the top side at the vertical gridline two squares to the right, i.e. at (2,3), so if its angle from the bottom side is θ, then tan θ = 3/2. Since tan α · tan θ = 1, the two acute angles α and θ are complementary, so α + θ = 90°. The image labels β as the angle between the two rays, so θ = α + β. Substitute to get α + (α + β) = 90°, hence 2α + β = 90°.

method.method_draft: Use a geometric complementary-triangles argument. From the image, the lower slanted ray forms a right triangle with horizontal leg 3 squares and vertical leg 2 squares, so α is the angle that this 3-by-2 triangle’s hypotenuse makes with the horizontal gridline. The upper slanted ray forms a right triangle with horizontal leg 2 squares and vertical leg 3 squares. These two right triangles have their legs interchanged. Therefore the angle the upper ray makes with the vertical gridline equals α, because it has the same opposite/adjacent leg ratio 2:3 as the lower ray’s angle with the horizontal. Since horizontal and vertical gridlines are perpendicular, the angle θ from the horizontal to the upper ray is 90° − α. The marked angle β is the difference between the upper and lower ray directions, so β = θ − α = 90° − 2α. Rearranging gives 2α + β = 90°.
